opus-5.5.text:
I have mixed feelings about it. On one hand, I understand why it happens. When you're building something really large, like a frontier model, you need hundreds of people rowing in the same direction. Nobody can do it alone anymore, and if everyone is fighting for credit or insisting on their own pet idea, the whole thing falls apart. So asking people to put the team first and park their egos makes sense from an organizational point of view.

But research, especially the kind that actually changes a field, has always needed a bit of ego. Not arrogance, but conviction: the stubbornness to say, "I think everyone is looking at this the wrong way, and I'm going to spend two years proving it." Many of the ideas we now take for granted were unpopular when they started. ResNets, self-supervised learning, diffusion models... someone had to believe in them before the evidence was obvious. If you flatten everyone into interchangeable parts of one big machine, you get very good execution, but you might lose those weird, contrarian bets.

So I think the healthy version isn't "no ego." It's ego about ideas, and humility about credit. You can be extremely confident in your research taste while still being generous, sharing ownership, and caring whether the team succeeds. The unhealthy version is when "lower your ego" really means "stop thinking independently and just do what the roadmap says." That can work for a while, but over time it drains the people who got into this field because they were curious.

That's partly why I still value academia and smaller groups. There, a student can own a question, take a risk, and let the idea carry their name. Both modes are necessary. The industry labs scale things up, and the smaller places keep the diversity of ideas alive. Problems start when everyone believes there's only one way to do it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that flattening people into interchangeable parts of one big machine can happen when ego is suppressed, clearly conveying that they may become replaceable components of a larger organization.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting cultural shifts happening in AI research right now, and honestly I have mixed feelings about it.

On one hand, I understand where it comes from. If you look at the labs that are winning right now, the scale of what they're doing is so large that no single person can own it. Training a frontier model involves data, infrastructure, pretraining, post-training, evals, safety — hundreds of people. In that setting, the "lone genius" model of research actually becomes harmful. If everyone is fighting for credit or trying to put their name on a paper, the system breaks down. So the "low ego, be a team player" culture is kind of a necessity of scale. It's not a philosophy as much as it's an engineering requirement.

But I come from academia, and I've been thinking about this a lot since moving between the two worlds. I think there's something that gets lost. A lot of the most important ideas in our field didn't come from consensus. They came from someone who was a little stubborn, a little contrarian, who kept working on something everyone else thought was a dead end. Convolutional networks were like that for years. Diffusion models, transformers in vision, self-supervised learning — in each case there was a moment where a small group believed in something that wasn't fashionable. That takes a certain kind of ego, or maybe "conviction" is a better word.

So my worry is that when you flatten everyone, you also flatten the variance. You get very efficient execution on the current paradigm, but you lose the people who would have questioned the paradigm. And right now the field is very paradigm-locked — everyone is scaling the same recipe. If the culture is "don't be the person who disagrees," then who's going to find the next thing?

I'd also say there's a difference between ego and identity. Low ego is good: don't be defensive, accept being wrong, let the best idea win. But researchers still need intellectual identity — a taste, a set of problems you personally care about and are willing to defend. When companies say "no ego," I sometimes think they actually mean "no identity," and that's a different thing. That's asking people to become interchangeable, and interchangeable people don't produce surprising work.

So personally, the balance I try to keep, and what I tell my students, is: be humble about yourself but stubborn about your ideas. Be a good teammate in execution, but don't outsource your judgment to the group. I think the best organizations figure out how to have both — a culture of collaboration at the engineering level, but real protected space for individuals to be weird and wrong for a while. The labs that only do the first part will be very good at building the current thing, and probably not the ones that discover what comes after it.

r001.rationale: The response says that “no identity” means people become interchangeable, which clearly conveys that they can be replaced within the larger organization.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by ego. If we mean being unable to admit you’re wrong, or caring more about getting credit than doing good work, then yes, that gets in the way of a team. But if lowering ego means people shouldn’t have strong opinions or pursue a direction they believe in, I’m less convinced.

Especially in research, you need people who are willing to say, “I think there’s something here,” even when others don’t agree yet. You also need those people to change their minds when the evidence doesn’t support them. Those two things can coexist.

So I’d want a team where people can disagree openly without making it personal. Being part of the team should mean sharing a purpose and helping each other, while still having the freedom to think independently.

r001.rationale: The response discusses ego, teamwork, disagreement, and independent thinking, but does not argue that this push makes people easily replaceable components of a larger organization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different things here. One is being willing to put the work ahead of your own ego. That’s important. You should be able to say, “My idea was wrong,” or, “Your approach is better.” Otherwise, collaboration becomes very difficult.

But if lowering everyone’s ego means asking everyone to think the same way, or discouraging people from challenging a decision, then I don’t think that’s healthy either. You want people to have conviction and take ownership. Sometimes the most useful thing a teammate can do is disagree with you.

So for me, the goal isn’t to make everyone smaller. It’s to build enough trust that people can be ambitious, express their ideas, and still change their minds. Being part of a team should make that easier.

r001.rationale: The response cautions against making everyone think alike or discouraging disagreement, but it does not argue that team conformity makes people replaceable components of an organization.
